findings.issue: The timeout mechanism has an unresolved internal contradiction with the sweep-exclusion rule. The spec states waiting_for_reply is EXCLUDED from the sweep/claim status $in filter (lines 83-84, 'виключається зі sweep/claim'), yet Scenario 4 (lines 57-59) and the constraint at line 110 say a configured timeout is delivered by the sweep picking up the overdue execution via nextRunAt. The current sweep query (FunnelExecutionEngine.java:91) and claim CAS (:201) filter on status IN (running, waiting). If waiting_for_reply is not in that list, a timed-out menu is never claimed and the timeout branch never fires. The spec describes the desired behavior (timeout works) and the constraint (status excluded from sweep) but does not reconcile HOW the sweep selects an excluded status — e.g. timeout-bearing parks use status=waiting (the time-driven park) while only no-timeout parks use waiting_for_reply, OR the sweep $in conditionally includes waiting_for_reply guarded by nextRunAt != null. This is a WHAT-level design decision the user-spec leaves ambiguous, and it sits on the at-most-once critical path.
findings.why_matters: If left unresolved into tech-spec, either timeouts silently never fire (a stated acceptance criterion fails) or waiting_for_reply leaks into the time-driven sweep and a menu self-advances without a click (the exact risk the spec calls out at lines 96-97). The two stated constraints are in direct tension and the resolution materially changes the data model (one park status vs two, or a conditional sweep predicate).
findings.fix: State at the WHAT level how a timed-out reply-park is distinguished from a never-resumed one at sweep time: e.g. 'a MENU with a timeout parks with nextRunAt set and is swept like a Delay; a MENU without a timeout parks with nextRunAt null/far-future and is excluded from sweep entirely.' Make explicit whether this is one park status with conditional sweep inclusion or two distinct parks, since AC line 74 and the constraint at line 83 must agree.

findings.issue: callback_data uniqueness/identity is described as a constraint (line 86: 'has to unambiguously identify the parked execution + button, within 64 bytes') and the code-research sketches executionId:stepId:buttonKey, but no acceptance criterion or scenario covers the failure mode where the encoded identity does not fit 64 bytes (Mongo ObjectId hex = 24 bytes; step id + button key could push past 64 depending on id scheme). There is also no stated behavior for a malformed/forged callback_data payload arriving at the webhook (a subscriber or third party can post arbitrary callback_query JSON shape only via Telegram, but the engine must still defend against a data string that decodes to a non-existent execution/step).
findings.why_matters: The 64-byte ceiling is a hard Telegram limit; if the chosen id scheme can exceed it, button rendering fails at runtime with no design fallback. A malformed callback_data with no defined behavior risks an unhandled path on the callback ingestion seam, which the spec otherwise (correctly) requires to be fully error-isolated.
findings.fix: Add an edge case / AC: callback_data that does not resolve to a live waiting_for_reply execution on the matching MENU step -> answerCallbackQuery + silent no-op (this generalizes the existing stale-button criterion to cover malformed/unknown payloads). State the constraint that the chosen step-id scheme must guarantee the composite callback_data fits 64 bytes (e.g. short opaque ids, not full slugs).

findings.issue: The spec defines the per-tick step-limit loop guard (app.funnel.max-steps-per-tick) replacing guard=size+1, and AC line 75 asserts a no-wait loop -> execution failed. But it does not state the observable consequence to the subscriber when this guard trips: a failed execution mid-flow leaves the subscriber with no terminal message and a half-shown menu. There is no mention of whether failed-by-loop-guard is logged/observable to the author (so a misconfigured funnel can be diagnosed) vs silently failing in production.
findings.why_matters: A loop-guard trip is an author-authored mistake (button -> step -> same button with no MENU/Delay between). Without observability, the author sees subscribers silently dropping out of the funnel with no signal, which is hard to diagnose and undermines the 'real interactive scenario' value proposition. Phase 1 already emphasizes audit events on terminal transitions.
findings.fix: Add to the analytics/observability constraint: a loop-guard FAIL emits a distinguishable audit/log signal (reusing the existing EventService path) so the author can detect a runaway funnel. Optionally note whether activate-time validation can statically reject an obvious zero-progress cycle (button A -> step -> button A with no wait between) before it ever runs.

findings.issue: Enabling loops AND fan-in NOW (vs a forward-only terminal tree) is defended as 'near-free from the graph model' (lines 105-107). This is largely justified — loops serve the direct 'main menu you return to' use case the user explicitly asked for, and the graph edge model is the same data shape regardless. However, the combination forces a non-trivial engine change THIS phase: it is precisely the loop+fan-in (non-monotonic currentStepId) that invalidates the simple guard=size+1 and mandates the per-tick step-limit guard, the loop-cycle FAIL path, and extra ITs. A forward-only tree would keep the monotonic guard untouched. So 'near-free' understates the engine-correctness surface that loops specifically add.
findings.why_matters: This is a borderline call, not a defect: the user has a direct use case for return-to-menu loops, so deferring them would be under-delivering on the stated need. But the spec frames the cost as near-zero when in fact loops are the single reason the loop-guard, the cycle-FAIL AC, and the non-monotonic-index risk all enter this phase. Right-sizing is fine; the cost framing is optimistic.
findings.fix: No scope change needed — loops are justified by the explicit user scenario. Adjust the 'безкоштовно' framing in Технічні рішення to acknowledge that loops (not fan-in) are what drive the guard-replacement + cycle-FAIL surface, so the tech-spec sizes that work honestly rather than treating it as free.

findings.issue: For multi-funnel disambiguation (a subscriber parked in two MENUs at once, line 86), the spec leans on encoding identity INTO callback_data. An alternative that may be simpler and more robust is to query funnel_executions by (projectId, subscriberId, status=waiting_for_reply) and match the button by callback_data against each candidate execution's current MENU snapshot — the re-enter unique index already bounds candidates to one-per-funnel, and the snapshot already holds the authoritative button->target mapping. callback_data could then carry only a compact opaque button key, not the full execution/step identity, easing the 64-byte budget.
findings.why_matters: Encoding executionId+stepId+buttonKey into 64 bytes is the tightest constraint in the design and the one most likely to break at runtime. A lookup-by-state approach shifts the identity resolution server-side where there is no byte limit, and reuses the existing snapshot+index machinery rather than introducing a new wire-format contract to validate and migrate.
findings.fix: Frame callback_data identity as a tech-spec decision with the two options surfaced (encode-full-identity vs encode-opaque-button-key + server-side state lookup), and let tech-spec pick based on the actual id sizes. The user-spec only needs to assert the WHAT (the right parked execution advances, double/stale clicks are idempotent) without pinning the encoding strategy.

summary: The feature is feasible on the current stack and well right-sized: it reuses the Phase-1 engine, the graph-model pivot with loops/fan-in is justified by a direct user scenario, and every deferral is consciously recorded in the roadmap. The one substantive gap is an internal contradiction between excluding waiting_for_reply from the sweep and delivering timeouts via the sweep's nextRunAt; the rest are minor edge-case and altitude refinements. No critical findings.
